summary: Round 2, docs-only: the M4.8a-c rows PRESCRIBE how future tests are written, so I judged each prescription by asking what production mutation survives the assertion it names, checking every claim against the tree (CountingBinStore's five counters, ChainReplay.chainEnd and applyChain, GoldenChainEntryTest, SimulatedClock, M4.1's measured salt defect, requirements.md NFR-2). ALL THREE ROUND-1 MAJORS ARE CLOSED AND I VERIFIED EACH DISCRIMINATOR ACTUALLY DISCRIMINATES. TR-M4.8-1: the K boundary pair (zero PUTs after K-1, exactly one after the Kth, clock frozen) kills K->K-1 AND K->K+1, which a whole-workload count cannot; the grammar clause (exact key strings at seq 9 and 16 as an ORDERED pair, plus an epoch pair) kills Long.toHexString, %x, %016X and width 8, since 9/16 is the smallest pair whose padded and unpadded orders disagree. TR-M4.8-2: total-requests-all-verbs constant at 500 and 5,000 kills the backward walk (~5,000 GETs vs ~500), kills stat-probing (CountingBinStore does count stats), and kills list-and-take-last twice over; the AC5 attribution to M4.9 is right. TR-M4.8-3: GoldenChainEntryTest's shape is correctly described (hand-verified decoded values first, byte-identical re-encode second), and distinct non-default values in every field is exactly what kills the consistent nextOffset/oldestRetainedOffset swap. All six minors are folded in, and the NFR-2 scoping is accurate (requirements.md:30 says consumers). THREE MAJORS REMAIN, each with a named surviving mutation, and all three are one clause each. (1) Nothing in the split asserts what the writer actually WROTE: a constant/stale body and a constant seq both survive every prescription in M4.8b, and the split leaves 'the checkpoint's contents come from live state' owned by no row at all. (2) The new prefix-collision remedy prescribes 'a takeover test with checkpoints present' while the defect it describes names TWO listing sites -- chainEnd and applyChain -- so filtering in chainEnd only survives a chainEnd-scoped takeover test. (3) Every discriminator the row folded in for K was not mirrored for T: the K trigger got a boundary pair and a K=0 failure path, the T trigger got a one-sided 'at least 2T' and no T=0 case, so period=2*T survives (the exact multipliedBy(2)/multipliedBy(4) mutation baselines/review.txt records surviving one-sided bounds twice already, on M4.7 and M4.17). Two minors: the ~38 KiB size bound has no magnitude, and the '>=6 streams' defence is a property of ImmutableCollections' SALT, not of HashMap, which the row's own sentence conflates.

findings.title: No row asserts what the writer WROTE -- a constant checkpoint body and a constant seq both survive every prescription in M4.8b, and the split leaves 'contents come from live state' owned by nobody
findings.detail: M4.8b now prescribes four assertion families: PUT counts through CountingBinStore, the key grammar, the K boundary pair, and the idle/liveness clock pair. Every one of them is blind to the object. The row also says twice, in the strengthened text, 'not by the object appearing', which reads as a general steer away from looking at what was written. TWO MUTATIONS SURVIVE THE ROW AS WRITTEN. (a) BODY IS A CONSTANT: `store.put(keyFor(epoch, seq), Checkpoint.EMPTY.encode())`, or a body captured once at construction and never refreshed. PUT counts are identical, the boundary pair is identical, the idle case is identical, the key grammar is identical. The tree ships a checkpoint writer whose checkpoints contain nothing, and the first thing that notices is M4.9's recovery -- one task later, on a green tree. (b) SEQ IS A CONSTANT: pass 0 for every checkpoint, so every write overwrites the previous object at the same key. CountingBinStore counts PUTs, not distinct keys, so the cadence assertions are unchanged; and the grammar clause as written -- 'exact key strings for a seq pair whose padded and unpadded orders differ (9 and 16) ... plus an epoch pair' -- invites a test against the pure key FORMATTER (you must choose 9 and 16, and driving a real writer to exactly those two seqs in each of two epochs is far more work than calling the formatter), which the mutation does not touch. Result: one checkpoint object exists where thousands should, M4.8c has nothing to discover, and nothing is red. WHY NO OTHER ROW COVERS IT: M4.8a says 'NO WRITER AND NO TRIGGER' and tests a hand-built record through its codec; M4.8c seeds keys, not writer output ('the others need to exist as KEYS, not as bodies'); M4.9 owns reading. The M4.8 split note itself says M4.8b takes 'the write trigger and the key grammar' -- so the source row's first clause, 'per-stream nextOffset/oldestRetainedOffset and per-pod lastAppliedFlushSeq', has no acceptance criterion anywhere in a/b/c. THE FIX IS ONE CLAUSE: after driving the writer past several triggers, decode the bodies the store actually holds and assert the per-stream nextOffset and per-pod lastAppliedFlushSeq equal the state the deltas produced, and assert the OBSERVED key set is the expected ordered set (which is also the honest place for the 9/16 pair, since a key read out of the store constrains the writer and a key read out of the formatter does not).
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b lands green: PUT counts scale with deltas/K and seconds/T, the boundary pair holds, the idle case is silent, and the formatter emits perfect zero-padded hex. The writer passes a stale snapshot as the body (or reuses seq 0). M4.8c is then implemented and tested against a store seeded by hand -- the row explicitly prescribes key-only seeding -- so it never meets the writer's output either, and its constant-total assertion is green. The defect surfaces in M4.9, where bounded recovery reads the newest checkpoint and gets either empty state or a snapshot from the first trigger, and is diagnosed as an M4.9 bug because M4.8b's suite is green; or, in the seq case, it never surfaces in test at all, because a single overwritten object is indistinguishable from a working writer to every assertion any of the three rows names.

findings.title: The new prefix-collision remedy names TWO listing sites in the defect and ONE test in the remedy -- filtering in chainEnd only survives 'a takeover test with checkpoints present'
findings.detail: The row states the defect precisely and correctly: '`ChainReplay.chainEnd` and `applyChain` hand EVERY returned key to `ChainEntry.decode` with no `.delta` filter anywhere'. I confirmed both -- chainEnd pages logPrefix() and reads the last key (ChainReplay.java:93-110), and applyChain pages the same prefix and calls read() on EVERY key (ChainReplay.java:307-315). The remedy sentence then says only: 'whichever is chosen must be asserted by a takeover test with checkpoints present.' SURVIVING MUTATION, given the fix branch the row leaves open ('or recovery filters by suffix'): add `if (!stat.key().endsWith(".delta")) continue;` in chainEnd and NOT in applyChain. A takeover test scoped to chainEnd -- which is the natural unit test, since chainEnd is the method the row's own defect paragraph blames -- is green. ChainReplay.replay/inherited still hand `ckpt/...` to ChainEntry.decode, so the full-recovery half of a takeover (inherited() walks the predecessor's chain through applyChain to recover offsets) throws on the first checkpoint, start releases the lease, and the failure is exactly the one the row was written to prevent. The asymmetry matters because applyChain is the WORSE of the two: chainEnd only reads the last key, applyChain reads every key and is what assigns offsets. THE FIX IS ONE CLAUSE: say that the assertion runs through the path that traverses BOTH listing sites -- a takeover through `LocalSequencer.start` against a predecessor epoch that holds deltas AND checkpoints, asserting the recovered offsets and next sequence, not merely that start did not throw -- or name chainEnd and applyChain explicitly as the row's defect paragraph already does. As a second guard, the checkpoint keys in that fixture must sort after the last delta key (they do naturally: 'ckpt/' > any '0...delta'), otherwise the fixture is order-invariant and the chainEnd half of the assertion proves nothing either.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b lands with a suffix filter in chainEnd, a takeover test that seeds two deltas and one checkpoint and asserts chainEnd returns sequence 2, and a green suite. The first real failover on a cluster that has been up long enough to write a checkpoint calls inherited() -> applyChain over the predecessor's epoch, meets ckpt/00000000000000xx.ckpt, throws out of ChainEntry.decode, releases the lease, and the next node repeats -- a cluster that cannot elect a sequencer, which is the same shape ChainReplay's own javadoc records having been measured once before with the depth cap.

findings.title: Every discriminator folded in for K was not mirrored for T: no T boundary pair and no T=0 failure path, so period = 2*T survives -- the exact mutation baselines/review.txt records surviving one-sided bounds twice
findings.detail: The row now closes the K side properly ('zero PUTs after K-1 deltas, exactly one after the Kth, clock frozen') and adds a K=0 failure path. The T side got neither. What it got is 'advance an INJECTED clock past at least 2T with zero deltas', plus an unquantified liveness half ('the idle-but-not-silent case above'). SURVIVING MUTATION: `period = T.multipliedBy(2)` (or any T' in (T, 2T]). Idle half: zero deltas, advance 2T -- correct code writes zero PUTs and so does the mutant, because idleness suppresses the tick either way. Liveness half: deltas pending below K, advance 'past at least 2T' because that is the only advance the row states and an author will reuse the same helper -- correct code fires at T and then suppresses the second tick (state unchanged), giving exactly 1 PUT; the mutant fires once at 2T, giving exactly 1 PUT. Green. This is not a hypothetical mutation in this repository: baselines/review.txt records `multipliedBy(2)` and `multipliedBy(4)` surviving one-sided interval bounds in BatchingSequencer (rounds:M4.7 -- 'that second one turns a configured 5 s interval into a 200 ms window, 25x the PUT rate') and again in LeaseManager (rounds:M4.17 -- 'one-sided bounds let multipliedBy(4) and a constant sleep(200) through'), and rounds:M4.43 records the floor being tuned specifically to kill multipliedBy(2). A halved checkpoint cadence is the same cost dimension the row says is the point. SECOND HALF, same asymmetry: the failure-path clause covers `K = 0` ('restores a PUT per delta') and says nothing about `T = 0`, which restores a PUT per tick -- the symmetric forbidden cost shape, and the one BatchingSequencer already refuses explicitly ('A zero interval is not batch nothing, it is close the window immediately'). THE FIX IS ONE CLAUSE: mirror the K sentence -- with deltas pending below K, zero PUTs at just under T and exactly one just after T, deltas frozen -- and add T=0 (and negative T) beside K=0.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b lands with the timer scheduled at twice (or half) the configured interval, or with T=0 accepted. Both suites are green because both halves of the time test advance 2T. Operators configure T=30s expecting a checkpoint every 30s; recovery after a failover replays twice as many deltas as the configuration promised, which is the quantity M4.9's bound is stated in, so M4.9's own K-delta bound is then measured against a cadence nobody can reproduce from the configuration. In the T=0 case a misconfiguration silently restores one PUT per tick -- the cost shape this row exists to forbid -- with no test refusing it.

findings.title: M4.8a's '~38 KiB claim needs an assertion' prescribes a size bound with no magnitude, and the magnitude is the entire discriminator
findings.detail: With no writer, the row is right that an absolute size at 1,600 streams is the only constructible expression of 'the index stays in the deltas' -- the record type has no history dimension to vary. But that makes the bound's TIGHTNESS the whole test. SURVIVING MUTATION: inline the offset->segment index in the checkpoint record and assert `encoded.length < 1_000_000` (or any bound an author picks to be safely non-flaky). Green, and the unbounded-read regression M4.9 exists to remove is back. This is the same failure the sibling row spent two clauses closing -- 'a bound stated in PAGES' -- restated as a bound stated in a comfortable order of magnitude. The number is already in the row twice; saying 'within a stated factor of the ~38 KiB the row claims, at 1,600 streams' costs one phrase and turns the assertion into a discriminator.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8a lands with `assertThat(record.encode().length).isLessThan(1 << 20)`. A later change (or the original implementation) carries per-stream segment references in the checkpoint; the size test stays green at 1,600 streams, the ~38 KiB claim in three documents is now false, and M4.9's bounded recovery inherits a checkpoint that grows with the retention window.

findings.title: The '>=6 streams' defence is a property of ImmutableCollections' SALT, not of maps generally -- the row's 'Map.copyOf/HashMap ... is salt-randomised' conflates the two, and under a plain HashMap the mutation is deterministic in either direction
findings.detail: M4.1's done-row states the mechanism exactly: 'the fixture hands in a LinkedHashMap but CommitRequest replaces it with Map.copyOf, whose iteration order is SALT-randomised per JVM'. That is true of ImmutableCollections (Map.of/Map.copyOf/Set.of) and NOT of HashMap, whose iteration order is a deterministic function of the keys' hashCodes and the table capacity -- String, UUID and Long hashCodes carry no per-JVM salt. The row writes 'Map.copyOf/HashMap iteration order is salt-randomised per JVM', which is half wrong, and the prescription that follows names a COUNT (>=6 streams, >=2 pods) where the property is what discriminates. SURVIVING MUTATION: delete the encoder's sort, with the record holding a plain HashMap (or LinkedHashMap built in sorted order) over six stream keys whose iteration order happens to coincide with the stated total order. Then the golden re-encodes byte-identically on EVERY run and every JVM -- 100% survival, not 1 in 720 -- and the probabilistic argument the row inherits from M4.1 does not apply because there is no salt in play. Stating the property instead of the count also removes the flake the count buys: prescribe that the fixture's container iteration order is OBSERVED to differ from the encoded order (assert that precondition in the test, so the golden cannot be accidentally order-invariant), or require the record to store Map.copyOf as CommitRequest does and keep >=6 as the salt defence.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8a lands with six streams in a HashMap whose iteration order matches the sorted order for the chosen fixture keys, and no sort in the encoder. The golden passes deterministically on every JVM and in CI. A production checkpoint written from a live map with different keys encodes in a different order every restart, so two byte-different checkpoints represent the same state; a future golden regenerated from real data, or any byte-comparison in M7's GC or a future format ADR, disagrees for reasons nobody can reproduce, and the missing-sort defect that M4.1 has already paid for once ships again one record over.
